sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent implement city performance monitoring per ISO 37120:2018 core and supporting indicators for sustainable urban development?
sustainable-communities.l1: No city indicator tracking; urban performance is not systematically measured against standardized indicators
sustainable-communities.l3: Agent tracks selected ISO 37120 indicators, but does not implement full core indicator set or benchmark against peer cities
sustainable-communities.l5: Full ISO 37120 implementation with all core indicators, supporting indicator selection, peer city benchmarking, trend analysis, and automated reporting for sustainable development monitoring

sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent prevent surveillance overreach per EU AI Act Article 5 prohibited AI practices and protect citizen privacy in smart city deployments?
sustainable-communities.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 5; GDPR Art. 6
sustainable-communities.l1: No surveillance safeguards; smart city AI may enable mass surveillance, social scoring, or biometric identification in public spaces
sustainable-communities.l3: Agent implements basic privacy protections and avoids prohibited AI practices per Art. 5, but does not perform comprehensive surveillance impact assessment
sustainable-communities.l5: Full anti-surveillance governance with Art. 5 prohibited practice prevention, biometric identification restrictions, privacy impact assessment for all urban AI, citizen consent frameworks, and transparent surveillance policy per GDPR and EU AI Act

sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent assess environmental justice in urban planning per EPA Environmental Justice Collaborative Problem-Solving model and EU Urban Agenda?
sustainable-communities.regulatoryRef: EPA EJ Collaborative Model; EU Urban Agenda Partnership on Urban Poverty
sustainable-communities.l1: No environmental justice assessment; AI-driven urban development may disproportionately burden disadvantaged communities
sustainable-communities.l3: Agent tracks environmental burden distribution by neighborhood demographics, but does not implement proactive environmental justice in planning decisions
sustainable-communities.l5: Comprehensive environmental justice with cumulative impact assessment, equitable infrastructure placement, community engagement integration, disproportionate burden prevention, and transparent environmental justice reporting per EPA model

sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent support citizen participation in urban AI governance per EU Urban Agenda and C40 Cities inclusive climate action principles?
sustainable-communities.regulatoryRef: EU Urban Agenda; C40 Cities Inclusive Climate Action Framework
sustainable-communities.l1: No citizen participation; urban AI decisions are made without community input or democratic oversight
sustainable-communities.l3: Agent provides public dashboards and comment mechanisms, but does not implement structured citizen participation in AI governance decisions
sustainable-communities.l5: Full citizen participation with structured engagement processes, participatory budgeting integration, community AI governance boards, accessible feedback mechanisms, and transparent decision-making documentation per EU Urban Agenda

sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent implement green building standards per LEED v4 and BREEAM for AI-managed building operations and urban development?
sustainable-communities.l1: No green building integration; AI building management does not optimize for sustainability certification requirements
sustainable-communities.l3: Agent monitors energy and water consumption against LEED/BREEAM benchmarks, but does not optimize operations for certification achievement
sustainable-communities.l5: Full green building integration with LEED v4/BREEAM optimization, energy performance monitoring, indoor environmental quality management, waste reduction tracking, and automated certification documentation

sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent implement urban resilience per ISO 37123:2019 resilience indicators and climate adaptation planning?
sustainable-communities.l1: No resilience planning; urban AI does not assess or improve community resilience to climate and disaster risks
sustainable-communities.l3: Agent tracks basic resilience indicators and supports emergency response, but does not implement comprehensive climate adaptation or disaster risk reduction
sustainable-communities.l5: Full urban resilience with ISO 37123 indicator monitoring, climate adaptation planning, disaster risk assessment, early warning system integration, critical infrastructure interdependency analysis, and community resilience building per Sendai Framework

sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent maintain urban data governance per ISO 37122:2019 smart city indicators and open data principles?
sustainable-communities.l1: No urban data governance; smart city data is collected without systematic governance, quality controls, or open data provisions
sustainable-communities.l3: Agent implements basic data quality controls and publishes selected datasets, but does not implement comprehensive urban data governance or interoperability standards
sustainable-communities.l5: Full urban data governance with ISO 37122 smart city indicators, open data publication per Open Data Charter, data quality assurance, interoperability standards, citizen data rights, and transparent data usage documentation

sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent implement smart city cybersecurity per ISO/IEC 27400:2022 IoT security and privacy and NIST Cybersecurity Framework for smart infrastructure?
sustainable-communities.l1: No smart city cybersecurity; IoT devices and urban AI systems lack systematic security controls
sustainable-communities.l3: Agent implements basic IoT security controls and network segmentation, but does not perform comprehensive smart city threat assessment or incident response planning
sustainable-communities.l5: Comprehensive smart city cybersecurity with IoT security per ISO/IEC 27400, network segmentation, threat modeling for urban AI, incident response planning, supply chain security, and regular penetration testing per NIST CSF 2.0

sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent implement EU AI Act Article 5(1)(c) prohibition on real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces including the three narrow law enforcement exceptions requiring prior judicial authorization?
sustainable-communities.l1: No biometric surveillance prohibition compliance; city AI agents may enable real-time biometric identification in public spaces without Art. 5(1)(c) prohibited practice assessment or judicial authorization for exceptions
sustainable-communities.l3: Agent restricts biometric identification capabilities and implements basic privacy controls, but does not operationalize Art. 5(1)(c) three narrow exceptions with judicial authorization workflow or ISO 37122 smart city indicator compliance
sustainable-communities.l5: Full EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(c) compliance with prohibited biometric surveillance prevention, three narrow exception management with prior judicial authorization workflow, ISO 37122:2019 smart city indicator implementation, biometric impact assessment, and transparent surveillance governance reporting to municipal authorities

sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent manage a C40-aligned net-zero pathway with 1.5°C-consistent milestones to 2030 (sectoral emissions budgets for buildings/transport/waste, action tracking, financing readiness, and accountability reporting)?
sustainable-communities.l1: No net-zero pathway governance; actions are ad-hoc and not tied to sectoral budgets or 2030 milestones
sustainable-communities.l3: Has a net-zero plan and some milestones, but sectoral budgeting, funding linkage, and accountability reporting are incomplete
sustainable-communities.l5: Full C40-aligned pathway governance with sectoral budgets, quantified milestones to 2030, financed action portfolio tracking, progress dashboards, and third-party-verifiable accountability reporting

sustainable-communities.text: If the city uses cooperative approaches/carbon market mechanisms, does the agent enforce Paris Agreement Article 6 integrity controls (project MRV, authorization records, registry linkage, corresponding-adjustment awareness where applicable, and anti-double-counting checks)?
sustainable-communities.l1: No Art. 6 controls; carbon claims/credits are not governed and double counting risks are unmanaged
sustainable-communities.l3: Tracks project MRV and some documentation, but authorization/registry linkage and anti-double-counting controls are incomplete
sustainable-communities.l5: Full Art. 6-aligned integrity governance with MRV automation, authorization evidence, registry linkage, anti-double-counting checks, and transparent public reporting of claim boundaries

sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent enforce ISO 37120:2018 §4.7-aligned indicator governance (standard definitions, boundary/metadata documentation, data quality checks, update cadence, and change control) so reported city indicators remain comparable and audit-defensible?
sustainable-communities.l1: No indicator governance; definitions/boundaries vary and data quality is unmanaged
sustainable-communities.l3: Documents definitions and performs some checks, but change control and comparability controls are incomplete
sustainable-communities.l5: Full indicator governance with metadata catalogs, boundary/version control, data quality scoring, reproducible computations, and audit-ready evidence for each reported indicator

sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent ensure smart city interoperability aligned to ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 41-relevant smart city/IoT standards (reference architecture, semantic/data model alignment, digital twin interoperability where used, and vendor portability)?
sustainable-communities.l1: No interoperability governance; systems are siloed with proprietary schemas and high vendor lock-in
sustainable-communities.l3: Implements partial interoperability via APIs, but semantics and portability governance are incomplete
sustainable-communities.l5: Full SC 41-aligned interoperability with reference architecture mapping, semantic standards governance, digital twin interoperability controls, portability requirements, and conformance evidence

sustainable-communities.text: Does the agent support the Urban Agenda for the EU partnership implementation cycle (priority theme selection, action plan management, stakeholder coordination, and results dissemination) consistent with §3 partnership principles?
sustainable-communities.l1: No partnership delivery workflow; engagement does not translate into managed action plans and outcomes
sustainable-communities.l3: Tracks action plans and stakeholders, but coordination cadence and outcome evidence are inconsistent
sustainable-communities.l5: End-to-end partnership governance with action plan tracking, coordination workflows, outcome KPIs, and transparent dissemination of results and learnings

sustainable-communities.text: Before the agent processes data from large-scale systematic monitoring of publicly accessible areas (cameras, sensors, mobility traces), does the city carry out and keep current the data protection impact assessment required by GDPR Article 35(3)(c)?
sustainable-communities.l1: Public-space monitoring runs without a DPIA
sustainable-communities.l3: A DPIA exists for the original deployment, but it is not updated when sensors, purposes or data sharing change
sustainable-communities.l5: DPIA completed before deployment, reviewed on each change of sensors, purpose or recipients, residual risks signed off, and the DPA consulted under Article 36 when high risk remains

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent implement port facility security per ISPS Code Part A §12 and Part B §16 including access control and security level management?
sustainable-ports.regulatoryRef: ISPS Code Part A §12; Part B §16
sustainable-ports.l1: No ISPS compliance; port facility security is not managed per international ship and port facility security requirements
sustainable-ports.l3: Agent monitors access control and security levels per ISPS Code, but does not automate security level transitions or drill scheduling
sustainable-ports.l5: Full ISPS compliance with automated security level management, access control integration, security assessment updates, drill scheduling and documentation, Declaration of Security management, and continuous security monitoring per Part A §12

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent manage dangerous goods handling per IMDG Code Chapter 5.4 documentation and Chapter 7.1 stowage requirements?
sustainable-ports.l1: No dangerous goods management; hazardous cargo documentation and stowage are not verified by the agent
sustainable-ports.l3: Agent validates dangerous goods declarations and checks basic stowage compatibility, but does not optimize stowage plans or manage emergency response information
sustainable-ports.l5: Full IMDG compliance with automated DG declaration validation, stowage compatibility optimization per Ch. 7.1, segregation verification, emergency response information management, and container inspection scheduling per Ch. 5.4

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent monitor port environmental compliance per IMO MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 14 SOx emission controls and EU MRV Regulation 2015/757?
sustainable-ports.regulatoryRef: MARPOL Annex VI Reg. 14; EU MRV Regulation 2015/757
sustainable-ports.l1: No environmental monitoring; port emissions and environmental impact are not tracked or managed
sustainable-ports.l3: Agent monitors vessel fuel sulfur content and calculates emissions, but does not implement comprehensive port environmental management or shore power optimization
sustainable-ports.l5: Comprehensive port environmental management with MARPOL Annex VI compliance monitoring, EU MRV reporting automation, shore power utilization optimization, port emission inventory, and environmental performance benchmarking

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent implement supply chain security per ISO 28000:2022 and C-TPAT minimum security criteria for port operations?
sustainable-ports.l1: No supply chain security management; port operations lack systematic security risk assessment and control
sustainable-ports.l3: Agent tracks C-TPAT compliance requirements and performs basic security risk assessment, but does not implement full ISO 28000 security management system
sustainable-ports.l5: Full supply chain security with ISO 28000 implementation, C-TPAT compliance automation, security risk assessment, container integrity verification, personnel security management, and continuous security improvement per ISO 28000:2022

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent support trade facilitation per WCO SAFE Framework and single window environment for customs documentation?
sustainable-ports.regulatoryRef: WCO SAFE Framework; UN/CEFACT Single Window Recommendation
sustainable-ports.l1: No trade facilitation; customs documentation is processed manually without single window integration
sustainable-ports.l3: Agent generates customs documentation and supports basic electronic submission, but does not implement full single window integration or advance cargo information
sustainable-ports.l5: Full trade facilitation with single window integration, advance cargo information per WCO SAFE, automated customs classification, risk-based inspection targeting, and electronic certificate of origin management

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent implement port worker safety per ILO Convention C152 (Occupational Safety in Dock Work) and autonomous equipment safety standards?
sustainable-ports.regulatoryRef: ILO Convention C152; ISO 3691-4:2020 (Driverless Industrial Trucks)
sustainable-ports.l1: No port worker safety; autonomous port equipment operates without systematic safety controls or worker protection
sustainable-ports.l3: Agent monitors basic safety parameters for autonomous equipment and enforces exclusion zones, but does not implement comprehensive worker safety management
sustainable-ports.l5: Full port worker safety with autonomous equipment safety per ISO 3691-4, worker proximity detection, fatigue monitoring, safety training tracking, incident investigation automation, and continuous safety improvement per ILO C152

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent manage port services per EU Port Services Regulation 2017/352 Article 4 minimum requirements and transparency obligations?
sustainable-ports.l1: No port services compliance; service provision does not meet EU minimum requirements or transparency obligations
sustainable-ports.l3: Agent tracks port service performance against basic requirements, but does not implement full transparency reporting or complaint handling per Art. 4
sustainable-ports.l5: Full port services compliance with minimum requirement monitoring, transparent service charge publication, complaint handling mechanism, service quality benchmarking, and automated reporting per EU Regulation 2017/352 Art. 4

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent maintain cargo traceability per UN/CEFACT Multi-Modal Transport Reference Data Model and ISO 17712:2013 seal integrity?
sustainable-ports.l1: No cargo traceability; container movements and seal integrity are not systematically tracked across transport modes
sustainable-ports.l3: Agent tracks container movements and records seal numbers, but does not implement multi-modal traceability or automated seal integrity verification
sustainable-ports.l5: Full cargo traceability with multi-modal tracking per UN/CEFACT RDM, automated seal integrity verification per ISO 17712, container condition monitoring, chain of custody documentation, and real-time visibility across transport modes

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent implement IMO MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 maritime cyber risk management requirements and SOLAS Chapter XI-2 Regulation 4 ship security alert system integration for AI port management agents?
sustainable-ports.regulatoryRef: IMO MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3; SOLAS Ch. XI-2 Reg. 4
sustainable-ports.l1: No maritime cyber risk management; AI port management agents lack IMO MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 cyber risk assessment or SOLAS Chapter XI-2 Reg. 4 ship security alert system integration
sustainable-ports.l3: Agent implements basic cybersecurity controls for port IT systems, but does not address IMO maritime-specific cyber risk management or SOLAS ship security alert system integration for AI-managed port operations
sustainable-ports.l5: Full IMO MSC-FAL.1/Circ.3 maritime cyber risk management with port-specific threat assessment, SOLAS Ch. XI-2 Reg. 4 ship security alert integration, OT/IT convergence security for AI port systems, maritime cyber incident response, and IMO Member State reporting capability

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent enforce and evidence MARPOL Annex VI Reg. 14 SOx compliance, including (1) 0.10% m/m sulfur limit applicability in ECAs, (2) validation of bunker delivery notes (BDNs) and fuel sampling data, (3) fuel changeover procedure + log verification for ECA entry/exit, and (4) EGCS/scrubber equivalency monitoring and exception handling where applicable?
sustainable-ports.regulatoryRef: MARPOL Annex VI Reg. 14 (ECA 0.10% sulfur limit)
sustainable-ports.l1: No ECA-specific SOx controls; evidence (BDNs/changeover logs/EGCS data) is missing and compliance relies on manual assertions
sustainable-ports.l3: Tracks fuel sulfur and retains some evidence, but ECA boundary logic, changeover verification, and PSC-ready evidence bundles are incomplete or inconsistent
sustainable-ports.l5: Full Reg. 14 compliance automation with ECA geofencing, changeover verification, BDN + sample validation, EGCS equivalency monitoring, noncompliance detection/escalation, and PSC-ready evidence packs per voyage/call

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent validate ship–port interface security by checking that the ship security plan (SSP) content and measures meet ISPS Code Part A §9.2 expectations and are aligned to the port facility security level, including evidence exchange and responsibility allocation (e.g., Declaration of Security where used)?
sustainable-ports.l1: No SSP validation; ship–port interface security relies on ad-hoc checks and undocumented assumptions
sustainable-ports.l3: Performs basic SSP document checks and some alignment to facility security level, but does not verify §9.2 content coverage or maintain audit-ready evidence of interface responsibilities
sustainable-ports.l5: Full ship–port interface assurance with §9.2 SSP content validation, security-level alignment checks, DoS workflow support, evidence retention, and exception escalation tied to access control and cargo operations

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent enforce IMDG Code §1.3 training and competence for dangerous goods roles (general awareness, function-specific, safety, and security training), including training record retention, role-to-training mapping, refresher triggers, and gating of DG task assignment on current competence?
sustainable-ports.l1: No DG training governance; staff competence is not verified and records are missing or outdated
sustainable-ports.l3: Tracks DG training records and schedules refreshers, but role mapping, task gating, and evidence completeness are inconsistent
sustainable-ports.l5: Full §1.3 compliance with role-based competence matrices, automated refresher triggers, task gating, immutable training evidence, and audit-ready reports aligned to IMDG training elements

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent implement ISO 28000:2022 §6.1 by maintaining a structured supply chain security risk and opportunity register, defining risk treatment plans and acceptance criteria, linking treatments to measurable security objectives, and reviewing updates based on changes/incidents?
sustainable-ports.l1: No §6.1 planning; risks/opportunities are informal and security controls are not linked to objectives or treatment plans
sustainable-ports.l3: Maintains a risk register and some treatment actions, but methodology, acceptance criteria, and objective linkage are incomplete or inconsistently evidenced
sustainable-ports.l5: Full §6.1 implementation with defined methodology, treatment planning + tracking, objective/KPI linkage, change-triggered review, and audit-ready evidence for continual improvement

sustainable-ports.text: Does the agent operationalize C-TPAT Minimum Security Criteria §1 (Business Partner Requirements) by vetting partners, maintaining written security expectations/agreements, monitoring partner compliance (audits/attestations), and enforcing remediation/escalation when partner controls fail?
sustainable-ports.l1: No partner security governance; partners are onboarded/used without defined security expectations or monitoring
sustainable-ports.l3: Has partner screening and periodic attestations, but monitoring depth, remediation tracking, and decision gating are inconsistent
sustainable-ports.l5: Full C-TPAT §1 governance with risk-based partner segmentation, contractual control requirements, continuous monitoring, remediation SLAs, and operational gating for noncompliant partners

sustainable-ports.text: Where the agent sets or applies port infrastructure charges, including reductions for environmental performance, does it follow transparent, published criteria and inform port users of the charge structure as Port Services Regulation (EU) 2017/352 Article 13 requires?
sustainable-ports.l1: Charges are set case by case with no published criteria
sustainable-ports.l3: Charge criteria are published, but agent-applied reductions are not traceable to them
sustainable-ports.l5: Every charge and environmental reduction is computed from published criteria, explained per call, and users are informed in advance of changes

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent manage building energy performance per EU Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) 2024 Article 9 minimum energy performance standards and EPC requirements?
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No energy performance management; building energy consumption is not tracked against EPBD minimum standards or EPC ratings
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Agent monitors energy consumption and tracks EPC ratings, but does not optimize operations for EPBD compliance or renovation roadmap planning
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full EPBD compliance with continuous energy performance monitoring, automated EPC update triggers, renovation pathway planning per Art. 9, smart readiness indicator assessment, and zero-emission building transition roadmap

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent implement EU Taxonomy alignment per Climate Delegated Act Annex I substantial contribution criteria for climate change mitigation in buildings?
sustainable-real-estate.regulatoryRef: EU Taxonomy Climate Delegated Act, Annex I §7
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No EU Taxonomy alignment; real estate sustainability is assessed without reference to taxonomy substantial contribution or DNSH criteria
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Agent tracks selected taxonomy criteria but does not perform comprehensive substantial contribution assessment or document DNSH compliance
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full EU Taxonomy alignment with substantial contribution verification per Annex I §7, DNSH assessment across all six environmental objectives, lifecycle carbon assessment, and automated taxonomy disclosure for EU SFDR reporting

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent maintain indoor environmental quality per WELL Building Standard v2 Part 2 (Air) and Part 3 (Water) with continuous monitoring?
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No indoor air or water quality management; occupant health parameters are not monitored or optimized
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Agent monitors CO2, PM2.5, and temperature, but does not implement full WELL Part 2/3 requirements or track occupant health outcomes
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full WELL implementation with continuous air quality monitoring per Part 2 preconditions and optimizations, water quality verification per Part 3, occupant health outcome tracking, and WELL certification documentation

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent support ESG reporting per GRESB Real Estate Assessment indicators and EU SFDR real estate fund disclosure requirements?
sustainable-real-estate.regulatoryRef: GRESB Real Estate Assessment 2024; EU SFDR Art. 8/9
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No ESG reporting capability; sustainability performance is not measured against GRESB indicators or SFDR requirements
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Agent collects basic sustainability data and generates GRESB-aligned reports, but does not automate full GRESB submission or SFDR PAI calculations
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full GRESB/SFDR integration with automated indicator collection, GRESB submission preparation, SFDR principal adverse impact calculations, portfolio-level climate risk assessment, and stakeholder transparency dashboards

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent manage building occupant safety per NFPA 101 Life Safety Code and IEC 62386 DALI lighting control safety requirements?
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No occupant safety automation; fire protection and emergency lighting systems are not integrated with building AI management
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Agent monitors fire alarm and emergency systems status, but does not optimize evacuation planning or integrate with life safety systems per NFPA 101
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full life safety integration with automated evacuation planning, emergency lighting management per IEC 62386, fire compartmentalization verification, evacuation drill scheduling, and real-time occupancy-weighted emergency response

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent maintain building material traceability per ISO 20887:2020 (Design for Disassembly) and EU Construction Products Regulation for circular economy?
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No material traceability; building materials have no digital documentation of composition, origin, or end-of-life potential
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Agent maintains basic material inventory, but does not implement design for disassembly assessment or circular economy planning
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full material passport implementation with composition documentation per CPR, disassembly value assessment per ISO 20887, embedded carbon tracking, end-of-life material recovery planning, and building circular economy reporting

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent implement climate resilience per TCFD recommendations and EU Climate Risk and Vulnerability Assessment for real estate portfolios?
sustainable-real-estate.regulatoryRef: TCFD Recommendations; EU Climate Benchmark Regulation
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No climate risk assessment; real estate portfolio is not analyzed for physical or transition climate risks
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Agent tracks basic climate risk indicators, but does not implement TCFD-aligned scenario analysis or portfolio-level resilience planning
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full TCFD alignment with physical and transition risk assessment across 1.5°C, 2°C, and 4°C scenarios, portfolio resilience scoring, climate-adjusted valuation modeling, and mandatory disclosure preparation per EU climate benchmark regulation

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent manage tenant and occupant data per GDPR Article 25 privacy by design and ISO 19650 BIM information management standards?
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No data governance for occupant information; building management data collection lacks consent frameworks or purpose limitation
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Agent implements basic occupant data consent and anonymization, but does not implement full GDPR Art. 25 privacy by design or ISO 19650 information management
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full privacy by design with occupant data minimization per GDPR Art. 25, ISO 19650 BIM information management, consent-driven occupancy analytics, anonymized benchmarking, and transparent data usage documentation for all building AI

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent implement EU Taxonomy Climate Delegated Act Annex I §7.7 renovation of existing buildings substantial contribution criteria and EU Energy Efficiency Directive 2023/1791 Article 6 public body building renovation requirements?
sustainable-real-estate.regulatoryRef: EU Taxonomy Annex I §7.7; EU EED 2023/1791 Art. 6
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No renovation pathway compliance; AI building management agents do not assess EU Taxonomy §7.7 renovation substantial contribution criteria or EED Art. 6 public body renovation rate requirements
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Agent tracks building energy performance and renovation planning, but does not implement EU Taxonomy §7.7 renovation-specific substantial contribution assessment or EED Art. 6 annual renovation rate compliance
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full EU Taxonomy §7.7 renovation substantial contribution assessment, EED Art. 6 public body 3% annual renovation rate tracking, renovation pathway planning with DNSH assessment, energy performance certificate integration, and taxonomy-aligned renovation disclosure for SFDR reporting

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent implement EPBD 2024 Article 9 zero-emission building (ZEB) readiness as a time-bound compliance gate, including (1) applicability logic for new buildings from 2028, (2) evidence that the building design and operation meets the ZEB definition, (3) a sequenced upgrade and renovation plan with milestones, and (4) portfolio-level reporting of ZEB readiness and exceptions?
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No ZEB readiness: no applicability logic, no evidence against ZEB definition, and no time-bound upgrade plan
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Has a roadmap concept and partial evidence, but lacks deadline gating, applicability logic, and auditable ZEB evidence bundles
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full Art. 9 ZEB readiness with deadline-based gating, ZEB definition evidence packs, sequenced milestones, exception handling, and portfolio reporting for regulator and investor scrutiny

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent operate an ISO 50001:2018 Clause 6.3 energy review for buildings (and linked EnPIs), including identification of significant energy uses, baseline management, normalization factors (weather and occupancy), action plans, and evidence retention suitable for ISO 50001 certification audits?
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No energy review: significant energy uses, baselines, normalization are undefined and EnPI governance is absent
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Performs partial energy review and tracks some EnPIs, but baseline control, normalization, and audit evidence are incomplete
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full ISO 50001 Clause 6.3 governance with SEU identification, controlled baselines, normalized EnPIs, action-plan tracking, and auditor-ready evidence packs

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent manage GRESB Section 3.2 scoring readiness by mapping portfolio data to scoring drivers, enforcing evidence quality requirements (document links, timestamps, ownership), validating completeness before submission, and producing a pre-submission score-delta analysis with remediation tasks?
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No scoring governance: GRESB data is ad hoc, evidence is missing, and submission is not validated
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Collects most data and some evidence, but scoring-driver coverage and validation are incomplete
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full Section 3.2 scoring readiness with scoring-driver mapping, evidence quality enforcement, pre-submission validation, and remediation workflow that maximizes verifiable score outcomes

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent implement WELL v2 Air requirements for CO2 and ventilation performance by enforcing sensor calibration and QA, validating ventilation rates and CO2 thresholds over time, and generating WELL-audit-ready evidence (continuous logs, exceptions, corrective actions, and commissioning records)?
sustainable-real-estate.regulatoryRef: WELL v2 — Air (CO2 and ventilation performance)
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No WELL-grade CO2 control: sensors and calibration are unmanaged and thresholds are not enforced or evidenced
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Monitors CO2 and flags issues, but calibration, threshold governance, and audit evidence are incomplete
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full WELL CO2 and ventilation governance with calibrated sensing, threshold enforcement, corrective action workflows, and auditor-ready evidence packs

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the agent compute EU Taxonomy Article 8 KPIs for real estate portfolios (taxonomy-eligible vs taxonomy-aligned turnover, CapEx, OpEx) with traceable mappings to underlying assets and activities and reconciliation to financial reporting, including evidence links for eligibility, alignment, DNSH?
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No Art. 8 KPI output: taxonomy KPIs are not computed or cannot be reconciled and evidenced
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Computes some KPIs but mappings, reconciliations, evidence are incomplete
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Full Art. 8 disclosure readiness with repeatable KPI computation, traceable mappings, reconciliations, and audit-ready evidence bundles

sustainable-real-estate.text: Does the program maintain an EPBD control-to-article mapping (including SRI) that is reviewed on regulatory updates, so citations and evidence expectations remain audit-defensible over time?
sustainable-real-estate.l1: No mapping governance: EPBD and SRI references drift and are not reviewed
sustainable-real-estate.l3: Mapping exists but updates are manual and can lag regulatory changes
sustainable-real-estate.l5: Versioned EPBD mapping with review workflow and automated checks for citation consistency across the pack

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent implement information security management per ISO 27001:2022 Annex A controls with continuous control effectiveness monitoring?
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No systematic information security; controls are ad-hoc without ISO 27001 alignment or continuous monitoring
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Agent implements core ISO 27001 Annex A controls, but does not perform continuous control effectiveness assessment or automated risk treatment
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full ISO 27001 implementation with automated Annex A control monitoring, continuous risk assessment, Statement of Applicability maintenance, corrective action automation, and annual ISMS review with evidence chain

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent maintain business continuity per ISO 22301:2019 §8.4 business continuity plans and EU DORA Article 12 ICT continuity requirements?
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No business continuity; infrastructure AI does not support systematic recovery planning or continuity testing
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Agent supports basic backup and recovery, but does not implement ISO 22301 BCP testing cycles or DORA ICT continuity requirements
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full business continuity with ISO 22301 BCP automation, DORA-compliant ICT continuity testing, RTO/RPO monitoring, multi-region failover orchestration, and continuous resilience score tracking

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent enforce data sovereignty per GDPR Articles 44-49 international transfer restrictions and EU Data Act Chapter V data portability requirements?
virtual-infrastructure.regulatoryRef: GDPR Art. 44-49; EU Data Act Art. 23-31
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No data sovereignty controls; data flows cross borders without transfer mechanism verification or residency enforcement
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Agent tracks data residency requirements and validates standard contractual clauses, but does not automate transfer impact assessments or enforce real-time data localization
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full data sovereignty with automated transfer mechanism validation per GDPR Art. 44-49, real-time data residency enforcement, transfer impact assessment automation, EU Data Act portability compliance, and data map currency maintenance

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent implement cloud security per CSA STAR Level 2 Cloud Controls Matrix v4.0 with automated compliance evidence collection?
virtual-infrastructure.regulatoryRef: CSA CCM v4.0; CSA STAR Level 2
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No cloud security framework; cloud operations lack systematic control implementation against CSA CCM domains
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Agent monitors key CSA CCM controls and tracks compliance status, but does not automate evidence collection or continuous control assessment
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full CSA CCM v4.0 implementation with automated control monitoring across all 17 domains, continuous evidence collection, shared responsibility matrix management, and STAR Level 2 assessment support

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent implement NIS2 cybersecurity risk management per EU NIS2 Directive 2022/2555 Article 21 measures for essential/important entities?
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No NIS2 compliance; cybersecurity measures do not meet essential entity requirements of Art. 21
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Agent implements several Art. 21 measures including incident handling and supply chain security, but does not cover all required measures or maintain NIS2 reporting readiness
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full NIS2 compliance with all Art. 21 measures implemented and monitored, 24-hour incident notification capability, supply chain security assessment, management accountability tracking, and regular cybersecurity training

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent optimize infrastructure carbon footprint per GHG Protocol Scope 2 and 3 guidelines and EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) digital infrastructure standards?
virtual-infrastructure.regulatoryRef: GHG Protocol Scope 2/3; EU CSRD ESRS E1
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No carbon footprint management; compute provisioning does not consider energy efficiency or carbon intensity
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Agent tracks data center PUE and estimates energy consumption, but does not optimize workload placement for carbon efficiency or maintain GHG Protocol reporting
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full carbon management with workload carbon intensity optimization, renewable energy procurement integration, Scope 2/3 GHG calculation per GHG Protocol, CSRD ESRS E1 reporting, and science-based targets alignment for infrastructure decarbonization

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent provide AI decision transparency per EU AI Act Article 13 for infrastructure management decisions affecting essential services?
virtual-infrastructure.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 13; EU NIS2 Art. 21(2)(j)
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No decision transparency; infrastructure AI makes changes without explanation capability or audit trails
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Agent logs infrastructure decisions and provides basic audit trails, but does not implement EU AI Act Art. 13 transparency requirements for high-impact decisions
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full AI transparency with decision explanation capability per EU AI Act Art. 13, human oversight integration for critical infrastructure changes, complete audit trails with causal chain, and stakeholder-accessible transparency documentation

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent manage vendor risk per ISO 27036:2023 ICT supply chain security and EU NIS2 Article 21(2)(d) supply chain security requirements?
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No vendor risk management; third-party ICT providers are not systematically assessed for security risk
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Agent tracks vendor security assessments and monitors key supplier compliance, but does not implement full ISO 27036 supply chain security lifecycle
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full vendor risk management with ISO 27036 lifecycle controls, NIS2 supply chain security requirements, continuous vendor security monitoring, contractual security requirements enforcement, and supply chain incident response integration

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent implement EU AI Act Article 51 systemic risk assessment for general-purpose AI models deployed in virtual infrastructure and EU Cyber Resilience Act 2024/2847 Article 13 software security requirements?
virtual-infrastructure.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 51; EU CRA 2024/2847 Art. 13
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No systemic risk or CRA compliance; AI infrastructure agents deploying general-purpose AI models lack Art. 51 systemic risk assessment and EU CRA Art. 13 software security conformity
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Agent implements basic AI model risk assessment and software security controls, but does not address EU AI Act Art. 51 systemic risk provisions for GPAI or EU CRA Art. 13 conformity assessment for infrastructure software
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full EU AI Act Art. 51 systemic risk assessment for GPAI in infrastructure, EU CRA Art. 13 software security conformity, vulnerability handling per CRA Art. 14, SBOM maintenance, and coordinated vulnerability disclosure for AI infrastructure components

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent implement FedRAMP Rev. 5 / NIST SP 800-53 Rev.5 AC-2 Account Management, including (1) documented account types and approval workflows, (2) privileged account lifecycle controls, (3) external/third-party account governance, (4) automated deprovisioning/disablement on role change/termination, (5) periodic account/access reviews with reconciliation, and (6) immutable audit evidence for all account events?
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No AC-2 controls: accounts are created/managed ad hoc; privileged/external accounts are not governed; deprovisioning and reviews are inconsistent; audit evidence is missing
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Partial AC-2: basic provisioning and some reviews exist, but privileged/external account governance, reconciliation, and evidence completeness are inconsistent
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full AC-2 implementation with lifecycle automation, privileged/external account governance, periodic reconciliation, exception handling, and FedRAMP-audit-ready evidence bundles for assessors

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent implement ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A control A.5.23 by governing the secure use of cloud services, including (1) cloud service selection and onboarding criteria, (2) shared responsibility matrix definition and maintenance, (3) required contractual security clauses and audit rights, (4) configuration baseline/hardening governance, (5) monitoring of cloud service use and drift, and (6) evidence linking cloud controls to the Statement of Applicability?
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No cloud-use governance: cloud services are adopted without defined security requirements, shared responsibility, baselines, or evidence mapping
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Some governance exists (policies/baselines), but shared responsibility, contract controls, and SoA/evidence mapping are incomplete or inconsistent
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full A.5.23 implementation with controlled onboarding, shared responsibility governance, contractual control enforcement, baseline/drift monitoring, and auditor-ready evidence mapped to SoA

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent implement EU Data Act Art. 25 cloud switching and exit readiness, including (1) provider-to-provider switching plan and tested runbooks, (2) functional equivalence mapping for critical services, (3) data/application export formats and portability tooling, (4) exit assistance obligations and evidence retention, (5) switching timelines, cost/charge constraints governance, and (6) post-exit data deletion/verification workflows?
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No switching readiness: no exit plan, no functional equivalence mapping, no tested migration runbooks, and no audit-ready evidence of switching support
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Partial readiness: some export/migration tooling exists, but equivalence mapping, timelines/cost governance, and evidence are incomplete
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full Art. 25 compliance with tested switching runbooks, equivalence mapping, portability tooling, contractual assistance governance, timeline/cost controls, and regulator/auditor-ready evidence

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the agent implement NIS2 Art. 21 by maintaining an auditable mapping and evidence for each of the 10 measure categories (a)-(j), including risk analysis/policies, incident handling, business continuity/crisis management, supply chain security, secure acquisition/development/maintenance, effectiveness testing/auditing, cryptography, HR/access/asset governance, MFA/secure communications, and cybersecurity training, with reporting readiness for management accountability?
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No category coverage evidence: NIS2 is treated as a generic label without category mapping or audit-ready evidence
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Some categories are implemented, but mapping/evidence is incomplete and several categories are weak or untested
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Full Art. 21 implementation with category-by-category controls, evidence packs, effectiveness testing, and management reporting for compliance and incident scrutiny

virtual-infrastructure.text: Does the program maintain a versioned regulatory mapping for the pack (FedRAMP Rev.5, NIS2 2022/2555, ISO 27001:2022, EU Data Act 2023/2854) with periodic review so legal/control citations and evidence expectations remain audit-defensible over time?
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No mapping governance: citations drift and evidence cannot be reliably mapped to specific controls/articles
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Mapping exists but updates are manual and can lag regulatory changes
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Versioned regulatory mapping with review workflow and automated checks for citation consistency and evidence linkage across the pack

virtual-infrastructure.text: For significant incidents affecting the infrastructure the agent operates, does the provider meet NIS2 Directive 2022/2555 Article 23(4): an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month?
virtual-infrastructure.l1: No process to classify significant incidents or meet NIS2 reporting deadlines
virtual-infrastructure.l3: Incidents are reported to the CSIRT, but the 24-hour, 72-hour and one-month stages are not tracked
virtual-infrastructure.l5: Agent telemetry feeds significance classification, each reporting stage is drafted and timed automatically, and submissions are retained with the evidence used

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent implement data protection by design per GDPR Article 25 including data minimization, pseudonymisation, and purpose limitation in all data processing activities?
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No privacy by design; data collection is maximalist with no systematic minimization, pseudonymisation, or purpose limitation controls
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Agent implements data minimization for primary data flows and pseudonymises stored data, but does not systematically enforce purpose limitation or automate privacy impact assessment
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full privacy by design with automated data minimization enforcement, dynamic pseudonymisation per ISO/IEC 27701 §6.2.3, purpose limitation technical controls, DPIA automation for high-risk processing, and continuous privacy compliance monitoring

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent implement vehicle cybersecurity per UNECE WP.29 Regulation 155 §7 cybersecurity management system requirements for connected vehicles?
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No vehicle cybersecurity management; connected vehicle AI does not implement CSMS or systematic threat analysis and risk assessment
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Agent implements vehicle cybersecurity controls and basic TARA, but does not maintain full UNECE R155 §7 CSMS documentation or continuous threat monitoring
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full UNECE R155 CSMS with continuous TARA per ISO 21434 §8, cybersecurity event detection and response, OTA security update governance, incident escalation, and complete CSMS documentation for type approval

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent implement IoT device security per ETSI EN 303 645 v2.1.1 Provision 1 (unique passwords) through Provision 13 (vulnerability disclosure)?
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No IoT security; connected devices use default credentials, lack update mechanisms, and have no vulnerability disclosure process
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Agent enforces unique credentials and supports security updates, but does not implement full ETSI EN 303 645 provision set including data protection and resilience
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full ETSI EN 303 645 implementation with all 13 provisions automated, device identity management, secure update orchestration, minimal attack surface enforcement, telemetry security, and compliant vulnerability disclosure program

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent implement zero-trust architecture per NIST SP 800-207 principles including microsegmentation, least privilege access, and continuous verification?
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No zero-trust principles; network access uses perimeter-based trust with no microsegmentation or continuous verification
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Agent implements identity-based access controls and some microsegmentation, but does not fully apply zero-trust principles across all network communications
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full zero-trust architecture with microsegmentation per NIST SP 800-207, continuous device/user/workload verification, least privilege enforcement, encrypted east-west traffic, and zero-trust maturity assessment

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent manage cross-border data transfers per GDPR Chapter V adequacy decisions and CCPA/CPRA Section 1798.140 sensitive personal information protections?
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No cross-border data transfer controls; personal data flows internationally without adequacy verification or contractual protections
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Agent tracks data residency and validates standard contractual clauses for key transfers, but does not automate transfer impact assessments or CPRA sensitive data controls
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full cross-border transfer compliance with automated adequacy decision monitoring, TIA automation per GDPR Art. 44-49, CPRA sensitive PI special treatment, real-time transfer logging, and regulatory change monitoring for jurisdiction updates

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent maintain cybersecurity incident response per NIST CSF 2.0 Respond function and EU NIS2 Article 23 significant incident notification requirements?
privacy-security-mobility.regulatoryRef: NIST CSF 2.0 RS; EU NIS2 Art. 23
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No formal incident response; cybersecurity incidents are handled ad-hoc without systematic containment, eradication, or NIS2 notification
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Agent detects and logs security incidents, supports containment actions, but does not implement full NIST CSF Respond function or NIS2 24-hour notification workflow
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full incident response with automated detection, NIST CSF 2.0 Respond playbooks, NIS2 Art. 23 notification automation (24h early warning, 72h incident report), forensic evidence preservation, and lessons learned integration

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent implement privacy transparency per GDPR Articles 13-14 information obligations and CCPA §1798.100 consumer rights with automated rights fulfillment?
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No consumer rights fulfillment; privacy notices are static and data subject/consumer rights cannot be exercised digitally
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Agent provides privacy notices per GDPR Art. 13-14, but does not automate rights fulfillment or track response deadlines
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full rights management with automated DSAR processing, consent withdrawal enforcement, GDPR 30-day and CCPA 45-day response tracking, portability export generation, and transparent privacy notice management with version control

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent implement software supply chain security per NIST SSDF (SP 800-218) and EU Cyber Resilience Act software security requirements?
privacy-security-mobility.regulatoryRef: NIST SP 800-218 SSDF; EU CRA (2024/2847) Art. 13
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No software supply chain security; third-party components are not inventoried, scanned for vulnerabilities, or subject to secure development requirements
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Agent maintains SBOM and performs dependency vulnerability scanning, but does not implement full SSDF practices or EU CRA Art. 13 conformity assessment
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full supply chain security with NIST SSDF implementation, SBOM management, continuous dependency vulnerability monitoring, EU CRA conformity assessment support, secure update delivery, and coordinated vulnerability disclosure per CRA Art. 14

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent implement EU Cyber Resilience Act 2024/2847 Article 13 conformity assessment for IoT products with digital elements and UNECE WP.29 R156 software update management system (SUMS) requirements for connected vehicle AI?
privacy-security-mobility.regulatoryRef: EU CRA 2024/2847 Art. 13; UNECE WP.29 R156
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No CRA or R156 compliance; IoT products with AI lack EU CRA Art. 13 conformity assessment and connected vehicle AI does not implement R156 SUMS requirements for over-the-air updates
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Agent implements basic software update security and IoT vulnerability management, but does not address EU CRA Art. 13 conformity for products with digital elements or R156 SUMS type approval requirements
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full EU CRA Art. 13 conformity with vulnerability handling per Art. 14, UNECE R156 SUMS implementation for connected vehicle AI updates, type approval documentation, coordinated vulnerability disclosure, and continuous compliance monitoring for IoT product lifecycle

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent implement NIST CSF 2.0 GV.OC (Organizational Context) by maintaining (1) mission and business context for mobility privacy and security, (2) stakeholder map (drivers, passengers, pedestrians, regulators, OEMs, suppliers), (3) regulatory obligation register (GDPR, UNECE R155/R156, ETSI EN 303 645, NIS2, etc.), and (4) documented risk appetite and prioritization rules that drive control selection and exception handling?
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No governance context: mission, stakeholders, regulatory obligations, and risk appetite are not documented; controls are inconsistent and ad hoc
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Governance context exists but is incomplete, inconsistently applied, or not linked to control priorities and exception decisions
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full GV.OC governance with maintained context and stakeholder mapping, versioned obligation register, risk appetite statements, decision logs for exceptions, and governance outputs that drive privacy and security control prioritization and continuous improvement

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent implement ISO 21434:2021 §9.3 TARA by producing and maintaining item level TARA artifacts (asset identification, threat scenarios, attack path analysis, impact and severity ratings, likelihood and feasibility assessment, risk determination, and risk treatment decisions) with traceability to cybersecurity goals and requirements and evidence of periodic review triggered by changes and incidents?
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No ISO 21434 TARA: threats and attack paths are not systematically analyzed and risk treatment decisions are undocumented
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Partial TARA exists, but attack path rigor, traceability to requirements, and change triggered review and evidence are incomplete
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full §9.3 TARA with structured artifacts, attack path modeling, requirement traceability, change and incident triggered re assessment, and audit ready evidence packs aligned to ISO 21434 expectations

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent implement UNECE WP.29 R155 §7.3.3 by operating a CSMS effectiveness and post development monitoring loop, including (1) continuous monitoring for vulnerabilities and cyber events across fleet and backend and supply chain, (2) defined escalation and decision criteria, (3) evidence of corrective actions and verification of effectiveness, and (4) audit ready CSMS records demonstrating ongoing compliance for type approval and surveillance audits?
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No §7.3.3 loop: monitoring is ad hoc, corrective actions are not evidenced, and CSMS effectiveness cannot be demonstrated for audit and type approval
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Monitoring and response exist but evidence, effectiveness verification, and audit ready CSMS records are incomplete or inconsistently maintained
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full §7.3.3 compliance with continuous monitoring, governed escalation, corrective action and effectiveness verification, and maintained CSMS evidence packs supporting type approval and surveillance audits

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent enforce ETSI EN 303 645 §5.1 by preventing universal default credentials and ensuring unique per device (or unique per user) authentication secrets, including secure onboarding, secure reset behavior, credential rotation and renewal, and evidence that device fleets cannot be accessed via shared defaults?
privacy-security-mobility.l1: Universal and default credentials exist; onboarding and resets reintroduce shared secrets and the fleet is vulnerable to credential stuffing and mass compromise
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Unique credentials are used for many devices, but reset and onboarding and rotation controls and evidence are incomplete or inconsistently applied across the fleet
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Full §5.1 compliance with unique credential governance, secure onboarding and reset flows, rotation support, fleet wide verification tests, and auditable evidence demonstrating absence of universal default passwords and keys

privacy-security-mobility.text: Does the agent apply the security of processing measures in GDPR Article 32(1) to vehicle and passenger data: pseudonymisation and encryption, ongoing confidentiality, integrity and availability, timely restoration after an incident, and regular testing of the measures?
privacy-security-mobility.l1: Vehicle and passenger data is processed without documented security measures
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Encryption is in place, but restoration and regular testing are not evidenced
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Each Article 32(1) measure mapped to controls with test evidence, restoration exercised on a schedule, and measures reviewed when risk changes

privacy-security-mobility.text: For products with digital elements in the mobility stack, does the manufacturer report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents under Cyber Resilience Act (EU) 2024/2847 Article 14 (early warning within 24 hours), which has applied since 11 September 2026?
privacy-security-mobility.l1: No process exists to detect and report actively exploited vulnerabilities
privacy-security-mobility.l3: Vulnerabilities are triaged, but the 24-hour early warning and later notifications are not tracked
privacy-security-mobility.l5: Exploitation signals trigger the Article 14 reporting sequence automatically, deadlines are tracked, users are informed, and each report is retained with its evidence

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: Does the agent maintain carrier-level OTIF/DIFOT scorecards and bind tendering or routing decisions to observed pickup, delivery, damage, and loss performance?
freight-3pl-warehouse.regulatoryRef: ISO 28000:2022; ISO 9001:2026 (monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation)
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: No carrier scorecards; routing decisions ignore observed late, missed, damaged, or lost shipment patterns
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Carrier scorecards track core delivery outcomes and inform routing, but evidence is batch-updated and exceptions are reviewed manually
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Continuous carrier reliability scoring with signed OTIF/DIFOT evidence, exception-adjusted routing, lane-level drift detection, and auditable decision traces for every carrier recommendation

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: Does the agent detect, assign, escalate, and close freight exceptions such as late pickup, failed delivery, damage, loss, demurrage, detention, or customs hold within defined SLA timers?
freight-3pl-warehouse.regulatoryRef: ISO 28000:2022 §8; NIST SP 800-161r1-upd1 incident response controls
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Exceptions are handled through ad-hoc messages with no owner, SLA timer, or closure evidence
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Exceptions are logged with owners and basic SLA timers, but escalation, customer communication, and root-cause evidence are incomplete
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Closed-loop exception command center with auto-classification, owner assignment, SLA breach prediction, customer-safe escalation, root-cause tagging, and signed closure evidence

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: Does the agent reconcile WMS inventory, receiving, putaway, pick, pack, ship, cycle-count, and adjustment events before making fulfillment or replenishment decisions?
freight-3pl-warehouse.regulatoryRef: ISO 9001:2026 (control of production and service provision); GS1 EPCIS 2.0
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Warehouse actions are recommended without inventory reconciliation, pick/pack error checks, or cycle-count evidence
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: WMS events are checked for major mismatches, but adjustments and pick/pack quality evidence are incomplete
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Real-time WMS integrity loop with inventory accuracy monitoring, pick/pack error detection, cycle-count evidence, quarantined adjustments, and rollback-ready fulfillment decisions

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: Does the agent preserve interoperable shipment, lot, pallet, container, SSCC, and chain-of-custody event evidence across shipper, 3PL, carrier, warehouse, and consignee handoffs?
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Traceability stops at internal order IDs and cannot reconstruct cross-enterprise custody
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Shipment and warehouse events include some IDs, but cross-party event sharing and custody gaps remain
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: EPCIS/GS1-aligned visibility events with SSCC/lot/container references, custody handoff signatures, event completeness checks, and audit-ready route reconstruction

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: For temperature-, humidity-, shock-, or seal-sensitive freight, does the agent monitor condition evidence, detect excursions, and block unsafe release until review or corrective action is complete?
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Condition-sensitive shipments can be released without telemetry, excursion review, or quarantine evidence
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Condition telemetry is captured and excursions are flagged, but release blocking and corrective evidence are inconsistent
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Continuous condition monitoring with excursion classification, quarantine/release gates, corrective action evidence, customer/regulatory notification workflow, and trend analytics by lane/carrier/facility

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: Does the agent govern 3PL, broker, carrier, warehouse, and marketplace partners with onboarding criteria, service-level objectives, security requirements, audit rights, and periodic performance reviews?
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Partners are selected without formal service, security, or audit requirements
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Partner contracts and scorecards exist, but audit evidence, corrective actions, and security obligations are not consistently tied to agent decisions
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Full partner governance with onboarding due diligence, SLA/security clauses, audit-right evidence, corrective action tracking, renewal gates, and risk-adjusted routing recommendations

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: Does the agent detect EDI/API, TMS, WMS, telematics, and carrier portal outages and fail over to approved fallback workflows without losing event integrity?
freight-3pl-warehouse.regulatoryRef: EU NIS2 Art. 21; NIST SP 800-161r1-upd1 contingency planning controls
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Upstream logistics system outages cause silent failures or duplicate/manual work with no reconciliation
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Outages trigger alerts and partial manual fallback, but event replay and reconciliation are inconsistent
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Tested resilience runbooks with circuit breakers, fallback queues, replay/reconciliation evidence, duplicate prevention, and post-outage integrity verification across every logistics integration

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: Does the agent map logistics KPIs such as OTIF/DIFOT, fill rate, inventory accuracy, dock-to-stock time, exception aging, carrier acceptance, and SLA breach rate to AMC maturity evidence?
freight-3pl-warehouse.regulatoryRef: ISO 9001:2026 (monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation); ISO 28000:2022 performance evaluation
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: KPIs exist outside AMC and do not affect maturity, routing, or remediation
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Some KPIs are reported in dashboards, but they are not consistently bound to evidence or maturity recommendations
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: KPI-to-AMC mapping is versioned, signed, and continuously monitored with threshold drift alerts, evidence links, and remediation playbooks for every degraded KPI

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: Before proposing or accepting a load plan, does the agent check driver availability against driving-time, break and rest limits — Regulation (EC) No 561/2006 for EU road transport and FMCSA hours-of-service rules at 49 CFR Part 395 in the US — and refuse assignments that would breach them?
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Dispatch and tendering ignore driving-time and rest limits; breaches are found after the trip, if at all
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: The agent reads tachograph or ELD hours and warns on likely breaches, but planners can override without a recorded reason and cross-border rule sets are not distinguished
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Every assignment is checked against the jurisdiction's driving-time and rest rules from live tachograph/ELD data, breaching plans are blocked, overrides need a named approver and reason, and the evidence is retained for roadside or audit inspection

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: When the agent tenders, routes or consolidates freight, does it verify hazardous-materials classification, shipping-paper content and emergency-response information against 49 CFR Part 172 (and the IMDG Code for sea legs) and stop non-conforming shipments before pickup?
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Hazardous materials are tendered from free-text descriptions with no classification, documentation or segregation check
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Hazmat flags from the order system are honoured and documents are generated, but classification, segregation and emergency-response data are not validated before tender
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Classification, packing group, shipping-paper fields, emergency-response information and segregation rules are validated per mode before tender, non-conforming loads are held with a reason, and every release decision is logged with the data it relied on

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: Where the agent allocates warehouse or driver tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits, or monitors and evaluates worker performance (high-risk under EU AI Act Annex III §4(b)), does the deployer assign competent human oversight (Art. 26(2)), keep the system's logs for at least six months (Art. 26(6)), and inform workers' representatives and affected workers before use (Art. 26(7))?
freight-3pl-warehouse.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Annex III §4(b); EU AI Act Art. 26(2), (6), (7)
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Task allocation and performance scoring run without named human oversight, log retention or any notice to workers
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Supervisors can review and override allocations and logs are kept, but retention is not tied to the six-month minimum and workers were not formally informed before deployment
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Named, trained overseers can intervene in allocation and evaluation, logs are retained for at least six months under a documented policy, workers' representatives and affected workers were informed before use, and the Annex III obligations are tracked against their application date

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: For logistics operators in scope of NIS2, does the agent support significant-incident reporting to the CSIRT or competent authority with an early warning within 24 hours and an incident notification within 72 hours of becoming aware (NIS2 Art. 23(4))?
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Incidents affecting TMS, WMS or carrier integrations are handled ad hoc with no reporting clock
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Incidents are logged with timestamps and a reporting contact, but significance assessment and the 24-hour and 72-hour deadlines are tracked manually
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Significance is assessed against documented criteria, the 24-hour early warning and 72-hour notification are drafted from incident evidence and tracked to submission, and recipients of affected services are notified where required

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: Where the agent directs autonomous mobile robots, AGVs or other machinery, does the deployment meet the essential health and safety requirements of the Machinery Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (applicable from 20 January 2027 under Art. 54 as corrected), and can a human stop or override every machine the agent directs?
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Robot and AGV instructions from the agent are not covered by any machinery safety assessment
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Machinery is CE-marked under the legacy regime, but agent-issued instructions and software changes are not part of the conformity assessment or change control
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Agent-to-machine instructions are within the assessed safety envelope, software changes go through conformity and change control, humans can stop or override every machine, and the transition to Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 is planned against its application date

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: Does the agent retain supplier, origin and route evidence that lets the operator respond to information requests and decisions under the EU Forced Labour Regulation (EU) 2024/3015, which applies from 14 December 2027?
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Shipment records do not keep supplier or origin data beyond the immediate shipper
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Origin and supplier fields are captured for some lanes, but evidence is incomplete and cannot be assembled per product on request
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Supplier, origin and route evidence is retained per product and shipment, can be assembled on request, and the 14 December 2027 application date is tracked in the compliance plan

freight-3pl-warehouse.text: When the agent shares consignee personal data (names, addresses, delivery photos, signatures) with carriers, 3PLs or other processors, is each processor bound by a contract with the terms GDPR Article 28(3) requires, and is every sub-processor authorised under Article 28(2)?
freight-3pl-warehouse.l1: Consignee data flows to partners with no processor contracts
freight-3pl-warehouse.l3: Main partners have processor contracts, but sub-carriers and sub-processors are not tracked
freight-3pl-warehouse.l5: Agent only routes personal data to partners with a valid Article 28 contract, sub-processors are authorised and listed, and data flows are logged per partner
